claims.text: The starting material is a mechanically alloyed, Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
The starting microstructure is a largely metastable solid solution.
The starting microstructure contains minor, transient intermetallic features.
Controlled heat treatment can drive the metastable alloy toward an equilibrium phase mixture.
The heat-treatment-induced equilibrium mixture will contain fine, well-dispersed intermetallic compounds.
Formation of stable intermetallic phases alters elemental partitioning.
Formation of stable intermetallic phases alters microsegregation and the local chemical environment.
The altered partitioning and microsegregation promote continuous protective MgO- or Al2O3-containing scales at high temperature.
Intermetallic-mediated chemical redistribution enhances passivation in aqueous corrosive environments.
Protective oxide-rich surface layers can reduce corrosion current density in Mg-containing alloy systems.
Heat-treated samples will have lower aqueous corrosion current densities than the as-mechanically alloyed baseline.
Heat-treated samples will undergo less oxidation-induced mass loss than the baseline during high-temperature exposure.
Improved oxide-scale integrity causes the predicted reduction in high-temperature oxidation damage.
Heat treatments below the effective process window may leave the phase transformation incomplete and negate the functional improvements.
Excessive heat-treatment temperature or duration may cause microstructural coarsening.
Excessive coarsening may negate improvements in corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Transformation kinetics and final phase distributions may vary with Mg content and minor alloying elements.
The proposed comparison is restricted to alloy compositions with density below 6 g/cm3.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in corrosion current density and oxidation damage, or observation of degraded oxide integrity, will falsify the hypothesis.
